statement: The National Geographic Society Headquarters is a historic complex of buildings in Washington, D.C., United States.

The complex was constructed in phases beginning in 1904 to house the offices and museum of the National Geographic Society, a scientific and educational nonprofit institution that has been headquartered in Washington since its 1888 founding.

The historical portion of the site consists of three buildings: the 1904 original structure Hubbard Hall, the adjoining Administration Building, of which the north wing was constructed during 1912–1913, and the south wing and central pavilion in 1932; and the 1963–1964 Stone Building.
A fourth building constructed in 1984 is too modern to be considered a contributing structure to the historical segment of the complex.
The National Geographic Society developed over time from a handful of Washington-area scientists into a substantial, internationally respected institution.
The group's headquarters grew along with the society, with the progressively larger buildings eventually occupying an entire half of a city block.
Their architectural styles evolved over time as well.
All buildings in the complex were designed by notable architects.
The 1963–64 Stone Building by Edward Durell Stone is considered a quality example of the New Formalism style.
The complex was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2023.
Hubbard Hall and the Administration Building had previously been listed on the register as contributing structures to the Sixteenth Street Historic District.
The site is also listed on the District of Columbia Inventory of Historic Sites.
As of 2025, the society still used the complex for its headquarters.
As of 2025, the society was constructing a 2026 expansion on the site.
The site comprises four buildings occupying the northern half of a long city block in central Washington, D.C., north of the White House.
The eastern boundary of the complex is 16th Street NW.
The western boundary of the complex is 17th Street NW.
The northern boundary of the complex is formed by M Street.
The southern boundary of the complex is formed by an alley bisecting the block.
The original headquarters structure, Hubbard Hall, is located on the northeastern corner of the block with its main entrance facing 16th Street.
The Administration Building also faces 16th Street.
The Administration Building was constructed just south of Hubbard Hall and extends south to the alley.
The Stone Building was built along 17th Street.
The Stone Building changed the site's primary orientation by having its main entrance open on 17th Street.
The complex's fourth building, constructed after the site's period of historical significance, was built on the site between the older three structures.
All four buildings are connected, either above or underground.
The National Geographic Society (NGS) held its first meeting in January 1888 at the Cosmos Club.
The Cosmos Club was a private D.C. gentlemen's club aimed at 'the advancement of its members in science, literature, and art'.
The society itself stated in its bylaws the goal of achieving the 'increase and diffusion of geographic knowledge'.
The group began with 33 members, many of whom were not scientists.
Gardiner Greene Hubbard was a co-founder and the first society president.
Hubbard was a lawyer and a recent transplant from Boston at the time of his election.
Hubbard led the group until his death in 1897.
Hubbard was succeeded as president by Alexander Graham Bell.
Alexander Graham Bell had married Hubbard's daughter Mabel while the two were in Boston.
Bell had been involved with the society since its early days.
Under Bell's leadership the NGS sought to become more populist.
The group had begun issuing a monthly magazine in 1896.
The magazine's contents were highly technical.
An early article in the magazine was titled 'The Classification of Geographic Forms by Genesis'.
Readership of the magazine suffered due to its highly technical content.
Bell hired the organization's first full-time employee, Gilbert H. Grosvenor, to take over as editor-in-chief of the magazine.
At Bell's direction, Grosvenor targeted a more general audience, partly by greatly increasing the amount of photography.
Grosvenor attempted not to 'lower the dignity of the Society'.
Bell and Grosvenor's changes were largely successful.
By 1900, the society's membership of roughly 2,700 was considered one of the highest of any of the world's scientific organizations.
In 1900, Hubbard's heirs announced that they had purchased a site at the corner of 16th and M Streets.
The purchased site was for the purpose of establishing a headquarters for the society and as a memorial to its founder.
The building was originally expected to cost $40,000, which is equivalent to $1.2 million in 2024.
The building was planned to have office space for the society and its magazine.
The building was planned to have a lecture hall for the group's smaller, more technical presentations.
The group's more popular lectures were being held at that time at a local church.
Following a bidding process, the architectural firm of Hornblower & Marshall was chosen to design the new building.
The new building was termed Hubbard Memorial Hall.
Mabel Bell was heavily involved with the planning process and had considerable influence over its final design.
The structure's cornerstone was laid in April 1902.
The cornerstone contains a box of documents concerning Hubbard's career and accomplishments.
The two-story building eventually cost over $75,000 to construct.
The building was sufficiently completed by October 1903 for its first floor offices to be occupied by the society's magazine.
A formal opening ceremony for the building was not held until March the following year.
Prior to that reception, Bell hosted a dinner in honor of W.J. McGee.
W.J. McGee was succeeding Bell as president.
Bell remained on the group's board of trustees until dying in 1922.
Bell contributed regularly to the group's magazine until dying in 1922.
Membership in the NGS surpassed 100,000 in 1911.
The NGS added 30,000 new members in 1911 alone.
By 1913, the society was using two branch offices in D.C. to house the clerks necessary to manage its rapid growth.
In December 1912, the group's board of managers approved an expansion of its headquarters.
They hired Arthur B. Heaton to design a new building.
The new building would technically be an annex as it was to be connected to Hubbard Hall via a hyphen.
The new structure was completed in October 1913 at a cost of $150,000.
The new structure stretched 80 feet (24 m) on 16th Street.
The new structure stretched 90 feet (27 m) to the rear.
The building contained clerical and office space as well as a cafeteria.
The building included a large third-floor office for Grosvenor, who was by then the institution's director.
As early as 1914, it was planned that the NGS would expand even further south on 16th Street.
In 1914, they purchased an additional 137 feet (42 m) of frontage on the road.
The eventual goal of the 1914 purchase was constructing a 3,000-seat auditorium.
By 1915, Heaton had drawn plans for the building.
The plans were to turn the 1913 annex into the northern wing of a two-wing structure.
The southern wing was to be designed in a complementary but slightly varied style.
An illustrated depiction from the time shows the building topped by a massive tower that would 'serve as a central landmark on 16th street'.
It was 1932 before any expansion on the site was completed.
Both the tower and auditorium were gone from the final design in 1932.
With its membership up to 1.25 million, the NGS announced its 16th Street expansion in April 1931.
Heaton was retained again along with the same builders who constructed the 1913 annex.
It was decided for the new construction to mirror that of 1913.
The new construction would become the southern wing and central pavilion of the Administration Building.
The 1913 building became the northern wing of the Administration Building.
Upon its completion, it was announced that the society's scientific collections would be kept in the new structure.
Fireproof vaults housing the group's 300,000 photographs of the world's geography were kept in the new structure.
The collection of 300,000 photographs was reportedly the largest in the world at the time.
The magazine's editorial offices were to be moved to the building as well.
The organization later established an exhibition space in the building called Explorers Hall.
Explorers Hall was free and open to the public during the week.
Explorers Hall housed a sampling of the group's holdings as well as occasional special exhibits.
The society's membership continued to grow through the middle of the 20th century.
By the time of Grosvenor's 1954 retirement, membership was up to 2.15 million.
In 1959, the group announced its intention to expand its headquarters again.
The 1959 expansion plan involved demolishing Hubbard Hall and building a new, seven-story building in its place.
A legal hitch concerning a 1905 transfer of ownership required the society to get court approval to raze Hubbard Hall.
The society was successful in attaining court approval to raze Hubbard Hall.
In March 1960, the NGS spent $1 million to purchase a four-story structure located at M and 17th Streets, behind its existing headquarters.
In June 1960, the NGS announced that the new headquarters building would be located at M and 17th Streets.
Hubbard Hall would remain standing after the 1960 announcement.
The NGS hired the architect Edward Durell Stone to design their new building.
Stone worked in the New Formalism style.
Stone intended for his design to meld with both the other NGS structures on the site and with Washington as a whole.
In his 1962 memoir The Evolution of an Architect, Stone wrote, 'Since the Society is a national institution, it was felt that the building should reflect the dignity of official Washington'.
The completed building stood ten stories tall.
The completed building cost nearly double the initial estimate.
Construction began in April 1961.
The finished structure was dedicated in January 1964.
President Lyndon B. Johnson spoke at the dedication ceremony.
President Johnson said of the new building, 'This imposing home stands not as a monument to the past but as a testament of confidence in—and enthusiasm for—the future'.
Following the dedication, The New York Times said that 'many regard the [Stone Building] as the most distinguished example of modern architecture in Washington'.
The Stone Building was Stone's first contribution to the architecture of Washington.
The 1971 Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on F Street was one of Stone's final major projects.
Explorers Hall was moved to the Stone Building.
Explorers Hall featured a rotating sphere measuring 11 feet (3.4 m) across and weighing 1,000 pounds (450 kg).
An operator manning a control panel used various special effects to project educational imagery on the globe.
One of the first three Picturephone booths in the United States was featured in the building.
Developed by Bell Laboratories, the Picturephone machine allowed for video phone calls to either of the other booths located at the time in New York and Chicago.
The Picturephone booth in the Stone Building was open to the public.
Calls could be made from the Stone Building booth at the rate of $16 for the first three minutes to New York.
Calls could be made from the Stone Building booth at the rate of $21 for the first three minutes to Chicago.
President Johnson's wife Lady Bird attended a 1964 inauguration ceremony for the new technology.
Lady Bird Johnson made a call to the Bell Labs scientist Elizabeth A. Wood in New York.
In 1978, both Hubbard Hall and the Administration Building were listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) as contributing structures to the Sixteenth Street Historic District.
Hubbard Hall, the Administration Building, and the Stone Building were collectively added to the District of Columbia Inventory of Historic Sites in 2022.
Hubbard Hall, the Administration Building, and the Stone Building were collectively added to the NRHP in 2023.
The headquarters has continued to expand since the completion of the Stone Building.
Another new structure was constructed in 1984 between the Stone and Administration buildings.
The nonprofit institution paid the building's full $50 million cost with cash.
The seven-story building was designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM).
The SOM building features horizontal massing with ziggurat-style setbacks.
The SOM building is considered too modern to be a contributing structure to the site's historical status because it was less than 50 years old when the complex was listed on the NRHP.
Hubbard Hall was renovated in 1984.
During the 1984 renovation of Hubbard Hall, the five N.C. Wyeth murals located inside were professionally restored.
By 2022, the site that had begun as a 7,659-square-foot (711.5 m2) building had grown by over 100 times to a complex the size of nearly 900,000 square feet (84,000 m2).
In 2024, it was announced that the society was yet again expanding its campus, now nicknamed 'Base Camp'.
The expansion includes the addition of a 100,000-square-foot (9,300 m2) museum.
According to the director of the group's building operations, the new construction 'extends into the campus's four existing buildings' including Hubbard Hall.
Construction on the museum began in mid-2022.
As of October 2024, the museum construction was scheduled to be completed in mid-2026.
The first purpose-built headquarters for the National Geographic Society was Hubbard Hall.
Hubbard Hall is a two-story, three-bay structure.
Hubbard Hall was designed by Hornblower & Marshall.
Hornblower & Marshall is a D.C.–based architectural firm responsible for a number of other listings on the National Register of Historic Places.
The firm chose an Italian Renaissance style for Hubbard Hall.
The Italian Renaissance style helped Hubbard Hall fit into what was a primarily residential neighborhood while still giving the appearance of an institutional building.
The exterior of Hubbard Hall is constructed with brick.
Both brick and mortar of Hubbard Hall are buff-colored, which makes the façade appear smooth.
Limestone is used for detailing on Hubbard Hall.
The hipped roof of Hubbard Hall is red terracotta.
The primary façade of Hubbard Hall includes a first-floor central entrance flanked by two single windows.
Above the entrance of Hubbard Hall is a stone tablet that reads 'NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SOCIETY' in all capital letters.
A row of decorative stone known as a stringcourse separates the first and second stories of Hubbard Hall.
Above the stringcourse on Hubbard Hall are three large arched windows and a central Juliet balcony.
Above the windows on Hubbard Hall, a horizontal strip, or frieze, is inscribed with 'GARDINER GREENE HUBBARD MEMORIAL' in all capitals.
The building's north elevation facing M Street consists of three single windows on the first story and one large arched window on the second.
The south elevation of Hubbard Hall faces the 1912 Administration Building.
The south elevation of Hubbard Hall features a recessed hyphen connecting it to the Administration Building.
The west elevation of Hubbard Hall has a two-story wing projecting from the building's central massing.
Since 1984, the west elevation of Hubbard Hall has closely faced the fourth, most recent building in the complex.
The interior of Hubbard Hall includes a first-floor vestibule and foyer equipped with marble floors and walls.
A marble split staircase ascends from the foyer of Hubbard Hall.
The staircase's landings are painted with murals by the artist N.C. Wyeth.
The murals symbolize 'the instinct for exploration and discovery'.
The paintings were a late addition to the building, having been commissioned in 1926 and installed the following year.
The rest of the first floor originally held offices for the organization's board members.
A basement contained darkrooms and filing rooms for developing and storing the group's photography.
An auditorium and library shared a large second story room that later served as a board room.
The second story room features a large carved stone fireplace.
The next building constructed in the complex was the Administration Building.
The Administration Building was designed by Arthur B. Heaton.
The Administration Building was built in two phases over a decade apart.
The completed Administration Building is a four-story, Neoclassical structure.
The Administration Building consists of a central pavilion flanked by five-bay wings.
The Administration Building is primarily constructed of buff-colored brick.
The buff-colored brick and a similar red terracotta roof provide continuity with Hubbard Hall despite the change in architectural style.
The building's primary elevation faces east on 16th Street.
Its entrance consists of three door openings cut into the pavilion's stone base.
The entrance is topped by a triangular enclosed pediment supported by Ionic columns that span the second and third stories.
A frieze is carved with the words 'NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SOCIETY' in all capitals on the Administration Building.
The structure's wings are designed in the form of a classical column.
The base of the wings consists of the basement and first story.
The shaft of the wings is made of the second and third stories.
The capital of the wings is the fourth story.
The base is separated from the upper levels by stringcourses.
The shaft features double-height windows and giant order pilasters.
A row of limestone molding known as a cornice projects below the capital.
The capital consists of windows separated by limestone panels decorated with carved limestone rosettes.
The Administration Building contained offices for the society.
Aside from the central lobby, the original floor plan and decorative elements of the Administration Building have been much altered since its construction.
The lobby features at least six types of marble.
Marble floors and walls are joined by red marble columns that extend upward to a plaster entablature and ceiling in the lobby.
A marble and brass world globe, the former logo of the society's magazine, is embossed in the center of the floor and surrounded by a marble-laid star in the lobby.
The Stone Building, also known as the Headquarters Building, was built between 1963–64.
It was designed by Edward Durell Stone in the New Formalism style.
The design aimed to create a modern building that still echoed the society's architectural history.
The ten-story building is built of reinforced concrete covered with white marble cladding.
Like the society's previous Administration Building, the Stone Building is designed in the form of a classical column.
A one-story base supports a nine-story shaft, topped by a flat-roofed capital in the Stone Building design.
The building's primary elevation faces 17th Street.
The Stone Building's primary elevation re-oriented the complex's primary entrance from east to west.
The structure's ground floor exterior features an array of marble piers that support the building's canopy and form an arcade.
The piers' resemblance to marble columns adds to the classicist appearance of the modernist building.
The primary entrance on 17th Street is composed of centered pairs of bronze doors.
Above the primary entrance on 17th Street is engraved 'National Geographic Society'.
The building's shaft is made up of rows of narrow, bronze-framed windows flanked by marble 'fins' projecting outward.
The windows and fins are separated horizontally by black granite spandrels.
The design emphasizes the building's vertical composition.
A flat, projecting roof caps the structure.
A flat, projecting roof was an element Stone used often in his work.
All four of the building's elevations share the same design motif.
All four elevations have ground floor entrances.
The building's interior was constructed with an array of office space, laboratories, exhibit halls, and a cafeteria.
While most of the interior has since undergone considerable changes, the main lobby retains much of its original appearance and fixtures.
The main lobby contains stone floors and marble walls.
The main lobby features a brass globe in its floor, much like the lobby of the Administration Building.
